catalog_quote: Stress tends to occur in one of the two first syllables of a word. Stress is not contrastive between words. When the stress occurs on the second syllable, the initial (unstressed) syllable has a tendency to be reduced. [...] Stress in disyllabic words tends to occur on the initial syllable. However, stress may occur on the final syllable under the following conditions: (1) An open syllable involving a complex nucleus occurring as the final syllable and one of the elements of the nucleus being a back vowel. /ɨreo/ [ɨ'rɛo] 'moon' /momoi/ [mo'moi] 'to swing' /undau/ [u'ndau] 'a fence' (2) A word final closed syllable, in which the final consonant is a bilabial, velar or glottal consonant. /suŋgrum/ [su'ŋgrum] 'type of grass' /surog/ [su'rog] 'a caterpillar' /karaʔ/ [ka'raʔ] 'I carry (fem. obj)' BUT /keri/ ['kɛri] 'I carry (masc. obj)' The words of three and four syllables have not fallen into a distinct pattern at this stage of analysis. One rule may be that stress occurs on the initial syllable unless the second syllable is a back vowel in which case the stress shifts to that syllable. This holds true unless all the syllables contain back vowels. Then the stress again occurs on the first syllable. /ʔurupwi/ [ʔu'rupwi] 'new' /kutuŋu/ ['kutuŋu] 'I hear' The second syllable when closed draws the stress to itself. /sumaŋyi/ [su'maŋyi] 'down'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress located within the first two syllables. Default initial stress; in disyllables stress goes to the final (=second) syllable if it is open with a complex (diphthongal) nucleus containing a back vowel (mo'moi, u'ndau) or closed by a bilabial/velar/glottal consonant (su'rog, ka'ra? vs 'keri). For 3-4 syllable words (few, possibly compounds) a tentative rule: initial unless the second syllable has a back vowel (then second), reverting to initial if all syllables have back vowels; a closed second syllable attracts stress (su'manyi). When stress is on the second syllable the initial syllable tends to reduce ([n̩'ta?i]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary stress described; 'secondary stress' in the paper is a clause-level prominence on one word per clause, and 'heavy stress' a sentence-level prominence on the word in focus.
new_statements.exceptions: "There are a few lexical items which do not follow these rules": /kumuŋge/ ['kumuŋgɛ] 'sister', /su?wewe/ [su'?wɛwɛ] 'hidden', /mamoge/ ['mamogɛ] 'hornbill', /bɨjeyl/ [bɨ'džeyi] 'proud'; polysyllabic rule explicitly tentative ('One rule may be..').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (1-4 syllables; longer ones possibly compounds 'receiving one primary stress'); transcriptions are isolation/citation forms; analysis based on Tring village speech. Authors frame stress within a discourse > sentence > clause > word hierarchy.
new_statements.identity_note: Sanders & Sanders 1980 state the analysis is based on nine months in the village of Tring (one of seven Kamasau villages; their companion dialect survey in the same volume, PL A-56:137-170, treats the village dialects). Language-level kama1367; no separate Glottolog dialect code used.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement from Sanders & Sanders 1980 (stress in one of the first two syllables, non-contrastive, disyllables usually initial but final under stated conditions): the 1994 grammar adds only (a) one primary stress per compound word and (b) stress staying on the root (second syllable) in prefixed forms of 'go', a small morphological detail consistent with the 1980 allowance for non-initial stress. It states no different placement and defers to 1980a, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the placement rule itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar gives no word-stress placement rule; its two-page phonology summary is a phoneme/orthography chart and explicitly refers the compiler to Sanders & Sanders 1980a (PL A-56:111-136) for the phonology. Incidental remarks only: a compound word carries exactly one primary phonological stress (stress is culminative at word level and diagnostic of wordhood); in the verb 'go', when the 3fs/3fp/3ns prefixes add a syllable (w-uso, r-uso, k-uso), stress stays on the root, i.e. on the second/final syllable of the disyllabic form rather than shifting to the added initial syllable. 'Phonological stress' on a fronted nominal (p.46) is sentence-level focus prominence, not word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the phrase 'one primary phonological stress' (p.9), implying non-primary stresses may exist; nothing further.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the w-uso remark (stress remains on the verb root when a prefixal syllable is added) is the only placement-specific statement.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources are by the same SIL team (Arden & Joy Sanders) and describe Wand Tuan = Kamasau [kms], East Sepik Province (villages Kenyari, Kamasau, Tring, Wau, Yibab, Wandomi, Wobu per the OPD); the grammar's sec. 1.2.1 discusses dialects but the description is of the language as a whole, examples mainly from the authors' village-based text corpus. No dialect-specific stress claims.

sources.note: Sec. 4 'Word' pp.114-115: stress not contrastive; falls on one of the first two syllables; disyllables initial by default but final if final syllable is open with a complex nucleus containing a back vowel, or closed by a bilabial/velar/glottal C; 3-4 syllable words tentatively initial unless 2nd syllable has a back vowel or is closed; a few lexical exceptions. Secs. 1-3 describe sentence-level heavy stress and clause-level secondary stress (focus).
